         Intervenors Solana Ranch Company, Solana Development, LP, Don Al Ringler, and

I.       INTRODUCTION

         This proceeding involves the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to amend their Certificates of Convenience and

Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line

Project, a proposed high-voltage transmission line spanning approximately 223 miles across

fifteen Texas counties. 1 The Solana Intervenors except to the ALJs’ alternative recommendation of

Route 894. Further, the due process deficiencies inherent in this CCN proceeding prevented full

development of the routing record. As set forth herein, if a route is selected, the record establishes

that Route 392, not Route 894, best satisfies the routing criteria the Commission must apply.

         (This section is not briefed.)

       D. Hearing on the Merits

       The Hearing on the Merits (“HOM”) was conducted over five days, June 8 through June

12, 2026, and required the parties to litigate 823 filed witness testimonies and 1,398 admitted

exhibits. Time for cross-examination in this proceeding was compressed past the point of

impinging on parties’ due process rights. Each attorney was allowed 13 minutes for cross

examination of the companies’ panel of eight witnesses. The time limit was enforced at 13 minutes

per law firm, effectively, whether that attorney or firm represented one party miles away from any

route of interest, multiple parties situated on one segment, or, as did the undersigned, two groups

of landowners, over 130 miles distant from one another, each bisected by the Applicants’ proposed

“best meets” route, and potentially impacted by other proposed links. Similarly, each attorney was

allowed only seven minutes to cross examine PUC Staff witness John Poole, and only three

minutes each for cross examination of any other intervenor witness.

        Put another way, the ALJs allotted a single block of cross-examination time for each

witness or panel, to be shared by all cross-examining parties represented by common counsel,

without regard to whether those parties were separately constituted intervenor groups with distinct

properties, witnesses, and routes at issue.

       Because the Solana Intervenors’ counsel also represented the Brady Creek Intervenors, an

unrelated intervenor group with property separated by more than 100 miles in the Study Area, the

Solana Intervenors and the Brady Creek Intervenors jointly moved on June 7, 2026, to allocate

 each group its own block of cross-examination time for the six witnesses or panels independently

designated by both groups, including the Applicants’ panel. 2

any party’s constitutional due-process rights. The PFD contends that the ALJs do not maintain

authority to resolve such constitutional questions, citing City of Dallas v. Stewart for the

proposition that an executive-branch agency such as SOAH lacks the power to resolve

constitutional challenges reserved exclusively to the judicial branch. 4

           The Solana Intervenors except to the ALJs’ reliance on Stewart as a basis for declining to

weigh the due-process consequences of the ALJs’ own procedural rulings in this PFD, or in any

contested CCN proceeding. Stewart is not a SOAH case and has nothing to do with an

administrative law judge’s ability to resolve constitutional challenges in contested CCN cases.

Stewart involved the Dallas Urban Rehabilitation Standards Board, a thirty-member board of lay

citizens with no legal training requirement, which found Heather Stewart’s abandoned residence

to be an urban nuisance and ordered it demolished. The city of Dallas demolished the house while

her appeal was still pending. After the demolition, Stewart brought an inverse-condemnation claim

under Article I, Section 17 of the Texas Constitution. The question before the Texas Supreme Court

in Stewart was whether the board’s prior nuisance finding could be given preclusive effect against

that later, independently filed takings claim in district court. 5 The Court held it could not, reasoning

that mixed questions of law and constitutionally relevant fact require de novo judicial review, and

that substantial-evidence review of a board’s finding did not adequately protect a takings

claimant’s rights.

            The board in Stewart was not composed of attorneys, did not conduct any contested-case

hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act, and afforded no right to cross-examination

comparable to the hearing conducted in this contested CCN proceeding. This proceeding, by

contrast, was conducted before Administrative Law Judges in a contested case with sworn

testimony, an evidentiary record, and the right to cross-examine adverse witnesses, now subject to

Commission review of the ALJs’ recommendation through exceptions such as these. The

constitutional questions at stake here are not whether SOAH may issue a binding constitutional

ruling that forecloses later judicial review, the concern Stewart addressed. The question is whether

the ALJs’ own ruling denying the Solana Intervenors a separate block of cross-examination time,

for example, and the numerous issues identified in the PFD compounding on these due process

concerns, leaves the Commission without a complete record on which to base the routing

recommendation that follows, and deprived the Solana Intervenors of their legal right to make that

record in the first place.

           That question does not require resolving the constitutional questions within the holding of

Stewart; it requires only that the Commission consider whether the record underlying the PFD’s

routing recommendation comports with the requirements of due process. The ALJs’ own decision

to summarize the due process concerns below, “to give the Commission and any reviewing court

the fullest record,” 6 demonstrates that, throughout a contested CCN docket, the ALJs are very

much engaged in handling constitutional questions. Said another way, whether the PFD chooses

to acknowledge SOAH’s jurisdiction or province to resolve constitutional questions in this

administration setting, constitutional questions implicating all intervenors’ due process rights are

         The Solana Intervenors were required to handle all the burdens of evidence, witnesses,

exhibits, and advocacy required throughout every stage of the proceeding, including discovery

requests and responses, deadlines, and motions, but when it came time for the HOM, they got short

shrift simply because their counsel also represented another intervenor group in this docket. That

violates due process. See State v. Crank, 666 S.W.2d 91 (Tex.1984) (“[T]he ultimate test of due

process of law in an administrative hearing is the presence or absence of rudiments of fair play

long known to our law.”); see also Lewis v. Metropolitan Savings and Loan Association, 550

S.W.2d 11 (Tex.1977) (“In the eyes of the law there is no hearing unless a fair opportunity is

afforded the parties to prove their case before an administrative agency.”).

        Had the ALJs granted the Solana Intervenors their own time allotment for cross-

examination consistent with their separate, independent status as an intervenor group, that record

would have been more fully developed before the ALJs reached the routing recommendation the

Solana Intervenors except to above and below.

separate cross-examination time compounded into a materially incomplete record on the issues

most contested in this case. 20 Setting aside any disagreement about the interpretation or application

of Stewart to this proceeding, the ALJs routinely address constitutional issues throughout this

proceeding, whether or not the Proposal for Decision acknowledges doing so.

 VIII. ROUTING CRITERIA (Issues 8-10)

           The ALJs chose to spend 46 pages of the PFD (100-146) doing little other than reciting

their understanding of certain parties’ positions on certain issues or sub-issues on the routing

question. Many intervenor parties worked hard and invested significant resources to put on

thoughtful cases on which route should be selected.

           That effort was rewarded by the ALJs with less than two pages of a routing

recommendation that did little to resolve the issues set out in the preceding 46 pages. On routing,

the Commission is not faced with whether a different outcome would amount to the Commission

substituting its analysis for that performed by the ALJs. Rather, on routing, if the Commission

reaches that phase of the case, the task is to perform the first analysis of the evidence. A rigorous

analysis of the evidence, and application of the statutory and regulatory factors, leavened with a

little common sense, will invariably result in the selection of a route other than 894.

           If the Commission selects a route in this case, it should be Route 392.

           A. Overview of Proposed Routes

                1. Route 894 (Central Corridor)

years. 22 The Solana Intervenors except to the PFD’s routing recommendation to the extent it

reaches a “best meets” determination for Route 894 without addressing this record.

           C. Community Values

           Although “community values” is not defined by statute or rule, the Commission has

defined the term to mean “a shared appreciation of an area or other mutual resource by a national,

regional, or local community,” and has described adverse effects on community values as “those

aspects of a proposed project that would significantly alter the use, enjoyment, or intrinsic value

attached to an important area or resources by a community.”38

           Solana Ranch is an approximately 8,000-acre property in Williamson and Bell Counties,

most of which is dedicated to an active development effort anticipating approximately 14,000

residential units together with commercial, civic, open space, and recreational uses. The Michaux

family, which has owned the Ranch since 1950, partnered with DMB Development in 2021 to

advance that plan, and the project reflects nearly six years of planning, entitlement, and
